chunks: And from him (Al-Shaykh) from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from Al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) sought forgiveness for the shavers three times. I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about Al-Tafath (shaving), and he said: 'It is shaving and what is on the skin of the human being.'

And we have clarified in what preceded of the book that whoever shortens his hair or mats it, shortening is not sufficient for him and shaving is obligatory upon him. And whoever restricts himself to shortening, a sheep's blood (fine) is incumbent upon him, so there is no basis for repeating it here. And for the woman, shortening by the amount of the fingernail is sufficient, he narrated.

key_terms.التَّفَثِ: Shaving or removing hair from the skin
key_terms.الْأَنْمُلَةِ: The fingernail (used here as a measure of length for shortening)
key_terms.الْمُحَلِّقِينَ: The shavers (those who completely remove hair)
key_terms.دَمُ شَاةٍ: Blood of a sheep (a specific fine/offering for incomplete ritual act)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between shaving and shortening hair in Hajj rulings according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the jurisprudential distinction between shaving (*halq*) and shortening (*taqsir*) during Hajj, emphasizing the Prophet’s thrice-repeated supplication for forgiveness for those who shave, a practice highly recommended in Shia tradition. It further specifies that while men must shave to fully discharge the obligation, shortening alone incurs a penalty, whereas women are exempted from shaving, with a minimal cut sufficing for them. The text also defines *tafsith* (hair removal) broadly to include any hair on the skin, reinforcing the comprehensive nature of ritual purity in Shia fiqh.
